1:
The day is the one just described. Gill places the withdrawal on the same day as the casting out of the dumb devil and the answer to the Pharisees who ascribed it to Satan,; the house was probably at Capernaum, and he left it because it would not hold the people. Augustine notes that the same day means either that these things followed at once or that little intervened. Robertson calls it the Busy Day and pictures the crowd stretched up and down the beach. Henry observes that Christ preached at both ends of the day and that, no Pharisees being present, he had better their room than their company; his pulpit was a ship, not made for the purpose as Ezra's was but converted to the use for want of a better. Clarke and Wesley both take the vessel for one kept on the lake for his use.

What a parable is gets four definitions. Clarke derives the word from casting one thing beside another, spiritual things compared with natural. Robertson takes it from placing alongside for measurement, separates it from the fable, which puts things as they are not in nature, and from the self-explaining allegory; he warns that the story usually carries one main point and that much heresy has come of pressing the details. Barnes gives four purposes at once: to make truth interesting, to reach ignorant hearers through the senses, to drive a rebuke home as Nathan did to David, and to hide from one part of the audience what another was meant to grasp. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish background that Clarke borrows from him, that no figure was more familiar, and that their religion might itself be called parabolical, folded up in ceremonies; he wonders that a people so dexterous at unfolding parables stuck in the outward shell of their own.

The four soils are read off the landscape. Ellicott insists on Eastern tillage: ground less perfectly cleared, a road crossing the field, rock under an inch or two of soil. The wayside is the skirt of that path, where the surface is hard and the birds that follow the sower reap at once; the stony place is a thin stratum over rock, where growth is rapid through the very circumstance that proves fatal; the thorns were invisible at sowing, their roots left below, so that the ears were slowly strangled in a survival not of the fittest but of the strongest. Barnes adds that the headland was simply what the plough had not touched, and that the seed on rock sprang up sooner not because it grew faster but because it had less earth to come through.

On the yield the commentators separate. Clarke takes the hundredfold as literal and marvellous, and reports his own sowing of oats at Millbrook, where one grain returned a hundred and nineteen and a divided wheat plant at Cambridge that gave twenty-one thousand ears. Ellicott notes the article, the good ground, and calls the hundredfold uncommon but not unheard of, citing Isaac. Barnes refuses the arithmetic altogether, since a parable teaches a general truth and its proportions should not be pressed.

The loss is laid where it belongs. Chrysostom says it came not of the sower but of the soil, and that with minds, unlike earth, rock may be made rich ground and thorns rooted out; he did not name the careless openly, lest he alienate them, and did not desist from sowing though he foresaw the waste. Calvin makes the same point of his own day, that if men who ran from far off like hungry persons are called barren soil we need not wonder the Gospel bears no fruit in many now. Wesley notes that the hindrances are named in the order they arrive and that it is not God's will that stops the seed but their own perverseness.
10:
The question comes in a pause. Ellicott places the disciples in the boat with him, the parable ended and the crowd out of hearing, and asks why parables now, and why to plain peasants rather than men sharpened in the rabbinic schools. Chrysostom admires their timing and their charity, that they did not ask before the multitude, and asked not why speakest thou to us but to them. Gill notes that more than the twelve were there. Calvin reads the complaint as generous: unable to grasp the parable, they concluded the people would grasp it as little.

What a mystery is gets settled first. Barnes insists the word means a thing concealed rather than a thing incomprehensible, naming as examples that the gospel was for the Gentiles and that the Messiah must die. Ellicott agrees: a secret kept from others and revealed to the initiated. Robertson traces the word to the initiate and behind him to the closing of the mouth notes the eastern mystery religions with their signs, and observes that Paul uses it of what was hidden and is now made known. Clarke widens it to the prophetic account of the Church folded into the parables that follow, given first to a few because those few would publish it.

The proverb of having divides them mildly. Clarke hears an everyday saying, that presents are made to the rich, and takes him that hath not for the poor man, a use he finds in Paul and in Aristophanes. Wesley and Barnes make it turn on improvement, Wesley calling it the grand rule of God's dealing with men, fixed as the pillars of heaven, and Barnes judging it just that opportunities long misimproved be withdrawn. Gill applies it inward, that true grace grows and the Spirit leads into all truth. Calvin refuses the reading of improvement here, taking the saying of God not forsaking the work of his own hands, while the reprobate, whose gifts have glitter but no root, waste away in their own poverty.

Whether the blindness is chosen or imposed is the chapter's hardest question. Chrysostom denies any necessity or fate: the knowledge is a gift from above, yet free will stands and the wording proves it, for he says not they see not but seeing they see not, since they had watched the devils go out and called it Beelzebub. Calvin holds the other end, that Christ deliberately spoke so as to be a riddle; the word is bright in its own nature and dark only as the world darkens it, yet the Lord keeps his secrets from the reprobate, and to call the apostles' privilege given excludes all merit. Augustine tries to hold both: they shut their own eyes and so caused God to shut them, but admits that the therefore they could not believe of the fourth Gospel presses hard, and concludes they had deserved it by earlier sins. Ellicott grants that Mark and Luke make the purpose penal and that this is the sense here, yet finds mercy under it, since a parable roused none of the enmity plain speech had roused and might set a man thinking. Lightfoot dates the stupor long before the passion, laid on the nation by Pharisaism and the sottishness of tradition, and sends the reader to Romans, where Paul repeats these words.

The blessing at the close is measured against the prophets. Chrysostom says the disciples saw not only what the Jews did not but what righteous men of old desired and never saw, who beheld by faith what these beheld by sight; and he notes that this joins the two Testaments, since the prophets would not have longed for Christ had they served another God. Clarke guards them from the inference: they were not shut out from salvation, only their time was not yet.
18:
The turn to the disciples is marked in the pronoun. Ellicott and Robertson both note that the ye is emphatic: what is withheld from the others is given to these. Barnes takes Mark's question, how then will ye know all parables, as a sign that this is among the simplest, expounded so they might learn to read the others; Gill hears in it a reproof for dulness in men who had received grace.

Calvin sets out the four kinds and then guards against arithmetic. One sort does not retain the seed, a second keeps it till it springs but not deep, in a third the blade is choked, and a fourth bears; but Christ fixed no number, and the produce of faith is not always alike. His sharpest point is who is left out: no open despiser appears here, only men with some appearance of docility, so that if the greater part even of these perish, the case of the rest grows dark. Ellicott traces the sequence in the first man: he hears, fails to take it in, the fault being moral rather than intellectual, and the evil one lifts it out of his memory. Robertson notes that Matthew speaks of the hearers as themselves the seed, and locates the blame exactly: not the seed in the heart, but the man who lets it be snatched.

On the wayside the four descriptions converge. Clarke observes that the three evangelists use three names for the same enemy, the tormentor, the adversary who opposes every purpose of amendment, and the one whose name means to dart through; and he makes the careless heart an open road where evil affections pass and repass unchecked, the devil's thoroughfare. Barnes says the gospel preached to hardened men lies like seed on the beaten path, never suffered to root. Robertson has the devil snatching like a bandit before the grain can sprout. Wesley divides the theft between inward and outward, thoughts of other things, or agents who raise other subjects when men should be weighing what they heard. Ellicott answers the oddity of birds in their multitude standing for one tempter: whatever makes men forget the truth does the enemy's work.

The stony ground draws the most feeling. Wesley allows the joy to be real, even transport, a man struck with the beauty of truth and drawn by preventing grace, and then finds no change in the ground of the heart, so that he discovers a thousand pretences for leaving a way so narrow. Clarke puts it as unbroken ground, the fallow never ploughed, a man who never felt his own sore and so has no motive strong enough to outweigh the scandal of the cross. Barnes says he is caught by the gospel as by something new and withers like rootless grain in the sun. Robertson calls it a mushroom growth, quick to sprout and quick to stumble, a picture of some converts in modern revivals; Ellicott presses the same point on method, that the more a system works by excitement the oftener such results appear. Gill alone insists this hearer is not careless like the first but settled and diligent, with some understanding.

The thorns and the harvest close it. Wesley distributes the thorns, cares to the poor, wealth to the rich, the desire of other things to all, and says of riches that they smile and betray, kiss and smite into hell. On the three yields Augustine offers orders of life, a hundredfold for martyrs, sixtyfold for virgins, thirtyfold for the married, whose warfare against their own lusts is the harder; or else three degrees in which death is despised, with endurance, with content and with gladness. He rejects a reading current in his day, that the saints will deliver thirty or sixty or a hundred souls at the judgment, because men were using it to promise themselves impunity.
24:
The second parable is set beside the first rather than against it. Ellicott puts the change of audience in order: the sower was expounded in the boat, and the tares, the mustard seed and the leaven are spoken again to the crowd on the shore. Gill marks the shift: the first showed the sorts of hearers, this the difference of members within churches. Wesley reads the kingdom of heaven here as the gospel dispensation, warns that is like means only that the thing may be illustrated, and insists God sowed nothing but good in his whole creation. Barnes and Clarke both take the field for the world, and Henry declines to separate the parable from its exposition, since each explains the other.

The weed is identified with some care. Robertson refuses the word tares and calls it darnel, a bastard wheat common in Palestine, like the true grain except that its seeds are black and indistinguishable from wheat until near harvest. Clarke hunts the term through the rabbinic writers, where it means grain that was right seed at the first and afterwards degenerated, adding from an old agricultural handbook that darnel baked into bread dims the eyes of those who eat it. Lightfoot presses the consequence: wheat and this weed are not reckoned seeds of different kinds, so the whole field was sown with wheat of one sort or the other, and the parable distinguishes not good men from bad but good Christians from bad.

The sleep is laid at the door of the watchmen. Augustine takes it of the heads of the Church lying supine and of the apostles having received the sleep of death. Clarke makes it lukewarm professors and indolent pastors, and turns on the pastors directly. Gill catalogues the sleep of a church at length, grace unexercised, duty done sluggishly, lukewarmness about Christ's cause, unconcern about sins of omission, and warns that churches in that state are likely to be filled with hypocrites and heretics. Wesley answers in a line, that they ought to have watched, for the Lord of the field sleepeth not. Barnes makes the darkness moral, the enemy working unseen where truth is preached, and says one of his arts in a revival is to spread plausible notions of piety until multitudes think themselves Christians who are not. Chrysostom orders it historically: error came after truth, false prophets after prophets and Antichrist after Christ, since the devil attempts nothing unless he sees something to imitate.

Who the weeds are is disputed. Augustine asks whether heretics are meant or Catholics of evil life, and decides for heretics, since the field is the world and not the Church; men who live badly in the same faith are better called chaff, which shares stem and root with the grain. Wesley makes the darnel the outside Christian who has the form of godliness without the power, and says the open sinner, having neither, is not properly figured here.

The refusal to weed is read three ways. Chrysostom takes it as a standing prohibition of putting heretics to death, since that would bring a war without end into the world. Ellicott sees only a question of timing: the householder is a pattern of patient wisdom who can defeat the malice but will choose his own hour, and while both are green men may mistake one for the other, or tear up both. Calvin turns the whole parable toward the discouraged, holding that its object is not to warn a mixed multitude but to keep the godly from despondency at the sight of good and bad confused, since many under pretence of zeal grow displeased and, finding absolute purity nowhere, withdraw. Wesley finds in the answer that an enemy hath done this a plain reply to the great question of the origin of evil, that God made men free but implanted no evil in them.
31:
These two are left unexplained. Ellicott takes that for deliberate training, since the disciples ask about the tares and never about these. Wesley marks the change of subject: the earlier parables concerned unfruitful hearers, these those who bear fruit. Gill says the first showed the state of the church to the end, this its small beginnings and large increase. Henry states the scope: the beginnings would be small, the latter end great.

The botany is handled with more caution than one expects. Ellicott observes that what we call mustard grows into nothing that could be called a tree, supposes the name covered any plant of that flavour, and says the least of all seeds is popular description not to be pressed with microscopic exactness. Robertson agrees: a tree not in nature but in size, an excusable exaggeration in popular speech. Clarke and Lightfoot bring the Talmud in evidence on the other side, the mustard stalk at Sichin whose broken bough roofed a potter's tent, and the rabbi who climbed into the one in his field as men climb a fig tree; Lightfoot adds the proverb that makes a grain of mustard the measure of the smallest thing. Barnes explains the difference by climate and kind, the plant taking years to become a tree where ours is an annual herb; Wesley reduces the superlative to idiom, one of the least.

What grows is read at two scales. Ellicott makes the seed here not the word but the Christian society itself, smaller at its sowing than any sect in Palestine and destined to outgrow every sect and kingdom; and he notices that the birds have changed sides since the first parable, standing now for the institutions of other races that shelter under it. Barnes allows both scales, piety in a renewed heart or the church, and adds a caution about young converts, who suppose they have much religion when they are like a blind man just restored to sight, whose sensation is vivid though he sees little distinctly. Clarke takes the inward scale: grace often begins in a single good desire. Calvin puts it to pastoral use: profane men despise the gospel because its ministers are of slender reputation and its converts of no consideration, and the Lord opened his reign with a despicable beginning on purpose, that his power might be better known by a progress nobody expected.

The leaven divides them sharply. Robertson says the likeness is to pervasive power and refuses the objection that leaven means corruption as exegetical jugglery, since the devil is called a lion and so is Christ; three measures is simply a common baking, and finding the Trinity in it is beside the mark. Augustine reads exactly as Robertson forbids, making the leaven love because it causes fermentation, the woman wisdom, and the three measures either heart and soul and mind, or the three degrees of fruitfulness, or Noah and Daniel and Job. Chrysostom keeps to the working: as leaven changes much flour into its own kind, so shall you change the world, and the word is hid rather than put, so that when you are cast down by enemies you shall overcome them. Lightfoot measures three sata against an ephah, Wesley calls it the usual baking, and Henry describes the action as certain, gradual and silent, the apostles hiding a handful of leaven in the mass of mankind.

The closing citation is defended. Chrysostom says the Evangelist quotes the prophet so nobody should think the method new, and notes Mark's qualification that he spoke as they were able to hear it. Augustine narrows the claim: he spake nothing without a parable does not mean he never used plain words, but that no discourse closed without one somewhere in it. Gill defends the ascription to Asaph, who is called a seer, vision being one kind of prophecy.
36:
The crowd is dismissed before the explanation. Chrysostom notes that he had spoken in parables to draw questions and got none, that no scribe followed him indoors, which shows they had followed only to catch him, and that the disciples now ask freely, passing over the leaven and the mustard seed as plain. Robertson renders the request as make it thoroughly clear now. Ellicott places it in Peter's house and infers they found this parable harder than the other two. Origen reads the movement the other way: when Jesus is with the multitudes he is not in his house, and it springs from his love of men to leave the house for those who cannot come to him. Clarke draws the moral, that men who attend only the public preaching will not understand the mysteries, which are learned by secret prayer.

On where the evil came from the answer is short and the commentators know it. Clarke says that after a thousand volumes on the origin of evil we shall know exactly what Christ says here, that an enemy hath done it; God could not produce sin, since nothing produces what is not in itself, and the enemy is deceitful, vigilant while men sleep, and hidden once he has sown. Calvin guards both ends: when wicked men are mingled with believers this is neither accident nor nature but the devil's trick, and saying so acquits God, not the men. Gill treats hypocrites and heretics in churches as proof of that enmity, and Ellicott notes how distinctly the parable recognises a personal power of evil.

Whether the field is the world or the Church is the real dispute. Robertson is emphatic that the article stands with both nouns, so field and world are coextensive, and that both the good seed and the darnel are sown in the world and not in the kingdom or the church; gathering out of his kingdom means out from the midst, since good and bad lie scattered together in every city. Augustine takes the other side plainly, that the kingdom here is the one that exists now, namely the Church. Ellicott stands between them: the parable is about the new order called the Church and explains the evil found in it, touching the wider world only by inference. Origen says the whole world might be called a field, and not the Church. Gill will have both, the whole world or the church in its several parts, while Chrysostom draws another conclusion from the same clause, that since he sows his own field this world is his.

What the tares stand for is narrowed twice. Augustine rejects the Manichaean reading that they are spurious passages inserted among the Scriptures, and makes them the children of the evil one. Ellicott rejects a second, that theologians who thought heresy the worst of evils naturally found heretics here; so far as heresy springs from self-will they are included, but the passage defines them as all things that offend and them which do iniquity. Wesley notes that the Greek is simply all scandals, whatever hindered the seed from rooting.

The harvest closes it. Chrysostom observes that the figure is used in two senses: elsewhere the fields are already white and one sows while another reaps, whereas here the same sows and reaps and the harvest is the end. Augustine finds it fitting that angels separate, since the good can discharge punishment with a good spirit as a judge does, while the wicked cannot perform offices of mercy. Barnes refuses to settle whether the furnace means material fire, insisting only that Christ would not hold out frightful images merely to terrify. Calvin admits how distressing it is that the Church is burdened with the reprobate to the end, and holds both halves, that patience is enjoined and that pastors must still labour to purify it.
44:
The audience has changed, and Origen makes something of it. These were spoken indoors to the disciples, and he asks whether they are parables at all, since Scripture attaches the word elsewhere and withholds it here. Wesley agrees that these are proposed peculiarly to the apostles. Chrysostom marks the change of theme: the leaven and the mustard seed showed the power of the preaching, these two its value.

What lies in the field is disputed. Clarke refuses a buried pot and argues for a mine, since there is no sense in buying a field for money a man might carry off as readily and as honestly; on his reading hid means kept secret until the purchase, and the gospel is a mine whose veins run everywhere through the Scriptures, so the field must be dug. Ellicott keeps the hoard and sets it in village life, where tales ran of men made suddenly rich by treasure concealed in war. Gill makes the treasure the Gospel rather than Christ or eternal life, hidden under the former dispensation, from the Gentiles, from the lost, and even from the elect before their calling. Henry divides the figure, Christ the treasure and the gospel the field, hid as milk in the breast, marrow in the bone, honey in the comb, and hid not in an enclosed garden but in an open field where anyone may dig.

The finder's honesty troubles them unequally. Barnes says plainly the conduct would be dishonest and integrity required him to tell the owner, but adds that Christ does not vindicate it and only describes how men actually get wealth, the point lying in the earnestness. Ellicott answers that parables do not concern themselves with such questions, any more than those of the unjust steward and the unjust judge, and notes that Jewish casuistry laid the rule of caution on the seller, so the disciples would not have been shocked. Robertson thinks the morality need not be bad at all, since a man might hide a find to keep it from thieves, and says it is not the point.

The pearl draws four readings. Chrysostom keeps it with the preaching: two things are required of a preacher, detachment and watchfulness, which the merchant denotes, and truth being one there is one pearl; a man carrying a pearl knows his wealth while others do not, since it hides in the hand for its smallness. Augustine offers Christ, the one man without sin, or love of the neighbour, in which the Apostle says all is comprehended, or the Word in which all things are contained, and concludes that whatever it is, its price is the possession of ourselves, since we can give nothing more. Gregory makes it the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, which a man having tasted leaves willingly what he loved before. Gill inverts the parable, making Christ the merchant who sought and purchased his elect, who are to him the pearl of great price. Origen presses the wording, that he sold not merely the pearls he had bought but everything he had, and turns aside into the natural history of pearls, those of the land and the better sort out of the sea.

The common lesson is drawn last. Calvin says both parables are meant to make believers prefer this to the whole world, since we are so captivated by its allurements that eternal life fades from view; the new life is little esteemed because it is hidden and lies in hope, and treasure is the apt figure because its worth is undiminished though buried out of sight. Henry finds there the reason so many slight it, that they look only at the surface of the field. Wesley makes the kingdom within a treasure hidden from the world and from the wisest in it, which a man having found hides deep in his heart.
47:
The net is the working kind. Ellicott distinguishes it from the hand-net of the earlier chapter and calls it the great drag-net, closing the day of parables on a lesson the fishermen could read at sight. Robertson gives the word that became seine and notes that as the field was the world, so this net takes every fish in the sea; he adds Homer's picture of the slain suitors lying like fish caught in nets of myriad meshes. Clarke assigns the parts: the net is the preaching, the sea the abyss of sin from which men are drawn, the hauling ashore the end of all things. Gill notes that a net does nothing unless cast, nor then unless the blessing follows. Gregory makes the net the Church, given into the hands of fishers, gathering wise and foolish, free and slave.

How far this repeats the tares is disputed. Barnes says it does not differ in meaning. Chrysostom finds the difference in the ground of ruin: in the tares men are lost by evil dogma, in the sower by inattention, here by an evil life, so that men drawn in the net and knowing God may still not be saved; the parable is added so that we should not think faith alone enough. Calvin takes both readings, that the Church while it lasts is a mixture and that the disciples are warned off the empty title of faith, since it is of little consequence to be gathered into the fold unless we are his own sheep. Ellicott names the same two thoughts, the mingling and the separation, but points at what the parable leaves out, that the casting of the net is meant to change what it catches, so that those who remain bad are bad by their own will.

Origen interrupts with a caution about the whole method. Likenesses are never likenesses in every respect: a painting in wax keeps surface and colour but not the hollows, a statue the hollows and not the colour, so when the kingdom is likened to a thing the comparison holds only where it is required. He then turns the figure on the Scriptures, the net being of variegated texture like the Old and the New woven of thoughts of every kind.

The question that follows is read with some warmth. Ellicott notes that the verb is the one used of the sower's hearers, that an apprehension at once intellectual and spiritual is what turns a disciple into a teacher, and finds a child-like readiness in their claim to have mastered everything. Barnes hears the kindness in it, and Chrysostom says he praised them for understanding.

The householder closes the chapter and divides the commentators. Augustine observes that he said not old and new, preferring the order of value to that of time, and turns it against the Manichaeans, who by keeping only the new promises remain in the old man of the flesh; he takes the two as the Testaments. Gregory objects directly: if the Testaments are meant we must deny that Abraham was learned, who knew the deeds without the words, and refuse Moses the name of householder, who composed one Testament without the words of the other; so the saying must look forward to men in the Church later. Lightfoot dissolves it into idiom: the schools debated whether new or old produce should be used in holy things, and a provident man kept both by him. Robertson keeps it as a character sketch, the merely rabbinical scribe producing only the old and stale while the disciple of the kingdom stays fresh-minded and still values the old. Wesley and Barnes end on the duty, that a prepared preacher holds a store out of which every sort of instruction can be brought, and that it is not to lie unemployed.
53:
Whether this is the visit Luke records is the first question. Ellicott admits a dislocation however the accounts are arranged, and concedes the near absence of trustworthy notes of sequence; but he declines to identify the two, since Luke sets his at the beginning and reports violence where here there is only amazement. Calvin agrees the narratives are nearly similar and not the same, and finds in the second rejection proof that the interval had reformed nobody. Augustine notes that the passage from the parables to what follows has no evident connexion, Mark and Luke both going on to a different event. Origen turns the opening clause against his own earlier argument: if what was spoken in the house were similitudes and not parables, the words when Jesus had finished these parables will not cover them.

The town and the astonishment are described plainly. Chrysostom identifies the country as Nazareth, not Capernaum, and observes that here the teaching rather than the miracles causes wonder. Clarke notes that they appear to have heard none of his doctrine until now, and draws the rule that those who should know Christ best are often most ignorant of him. Barnes adds from Mark that it was a Sabbath, any Jew called on by the minister having the right to address the people. Henry marks the persistence, that his countrymen had rejected him once and he came again, since Christ does not take refusers at their first word, and quotes Seneca that a man loves his country not because it is beautiful but because it is his own.

Two things are cast at him. Henry puts the first as want of an academical education, and says prejudiced spirits enquire more into a man's rise than into his reasons, turning against him what was really for him. Chrysostom answers that illustrious sons came of ignoble fathers, David of a husbandman and Amos of a shepherd, so they ought to have honoured him the more. Origen reads their question as unwilling testimony, since whence hath this man this wisdom concedes a surpassing wisdom, spoken by men who did not know he was a virgin's son. Robertson puts it plainly: people are often baffled how a boy they knew became the man he seems. Calvin says they ought to have seen the hand of God, and that ingratitude dazzled them instead.

The trade itself is the second reproach, and the commentators take it up gladly. Clarke reports the old Latin copies that read the son of Joseph the carpenter, thinks our Lord worked at the trade through the thirty years, and remarks that an honest trade is no discredit. Barnes takes Mark's blunter the carpenter as near proof that he worked at it till thirty. Gill weighs the word, which covers any craftsman, and tells of the schoolmaster at Antioch who, asked in mockery what the carpenter's son was doing, answered that he was making a coffin for Julian.

The brethren divide them. Clarke allows that Hebrew usage can stretch the word to near relations but doubts it, and asks why another family's children should share a reproach aimed at one household. Wesley makes them kinsmen, sons of Mary the wife of Cleophas. Augustine thinks it no wonder that kinsmen on the mother's side should be so called, when men who took him for Joseph's son called others brethren through Joseph. Gill reports Epiphanius making the sisters Joseph's daughters by an earlier wife, while Robertson takes them for younger half brothers and sisters. On the scarcity of miracles Chrysostom says he looked not to display but to profit, and worked a few so none could plead that none were done; Robertson has their disbelief blocking the power, and Wesley turns it on his own readers, that mighty works are scarce now not because faith is unplanted but because unbelief prevails.
